title: Research Bite #27: Education and Intelligence: Pity the Poor Teacher
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #27 covers Douglas Detterman's provocative "Education and Intelligence: Pity the Poor Teacher," which argues that student characteristics -- above all general cognitive ability -- explain far more of the variance in academic outcomes than teachers or schools do. Drawing on decades of research including the Coleman Report and twin studies, Detterman estimates schools account for roughly 10% of the variance in achievement in developed countries, and that teachers within that figure account for only about 1-8%, while as much as 90% of the variance is associated with students themselves, with 50-80% of that attributable to differences in intelligence. His thought experiment is the sharpest illustration: predicted correlations between average student ability and achievement run as high as 0.95, while predicted correlations between teacher quality and student gains top out around 0.32. Detterman isn't arguing teachers don't matter, but that education research and reform have overweighted teacher-focused interventions relative to their actual statistical leverage, and that progress requires taking student-level cognitive differences seriously rather than treating them as background noise. Barton frames the classroom takeaway as one of realistic expectations: teachers are working within constraints substantially set by factors outside their control, which argues for appreciating the difficulty of the job rather than assigning teachers the blame -- or credit -- for outcomes mostly driven by who is sitting in the room.
points: The headline statistic -- teachers account for only 1-7% of variance in academic outcomes, versus up to 90% associated with student characteristics -- is a direct challenge to teacher-centered narratives of school improvement.

Detterman's thought experiment puts numbers on the imbalance: predicted correlation between student ability and achievement (up to 0.95) dwarfs the predicted correlation between teacher quality and student gains (up to 0.32).
The argument isn't that teachers don't matter, but that decades of research and reform have overweighted teacher-focused interventions relative to their actual measured leverage on outcomes.

The implication for realistic expectations: teachers operate within constraints substantially set by student characteristics outside their control, which cuts against both blaming and over-crediting teachers for outcomes.
quotes: The author contends that student characteristics, particularly general cognitive ability or intelligence, account for the vast majority of variance in educational outcomes, far outweighing the impact of teachers or schools.

Research spanning decades, including the Coleman Report and twin studies, supports this claim, indicating that school and teacher-related factors contribute only a small percentage to overall achievement.
The source suggests that teachers account for only 1% to 7% of the total variance in academic achievement at every level of education.
As much as 90% of the variance in educational outcomes is associated with students, and a substantial portion of this (50% to 80%) is due to differences in intelligence.

The predicted correlation between student achievement and mean student ability could be as high as 0.95, while the correlation between teacher quality and average student gain is predicted to never exceed 0.32.
Educational gain will be best predicted by student abilities (up to r = 0.95) and much less by teachers’ skill (up to r = 0.32).
It is argued that blaming teachers for all the problems of the educational system is inappropriate.
